Actually magnesium sulfide is white. But Mg2+ forms white precipitate with KOH (Mg(OH)2 white) and does not dissolve in NH3 (Mg(OH)2 is insoluble in NH3). So Mg2+ possible. Also Al2S3? Aluminum sulfide hydrolyzes to produce H2S, not typical. So white precipitate with (NH4)2S suggests maybe MgS (white). So cation could be Mg2+. Let's test further: we can test with flame test again? Mg gives no flame color. So consistent. Also we can test with HCl to see if precipitate dissolves? Not needed.

We have narrowed to Mg2+ or maybe Ca2+? CaS is white? Calcium sulfide is white. Ca(OH)2 is white and does not dissolve in NH3. So Ca2+ also possible. But Ca2+ would give a flame orange-red (characteristic). Flame test gave no color, so Ca2+ unlikely. Ba2+ gives green flame, also not observed. Sr2+ gives red flame. So those are out. Pb2+ gives no flame color? Lead gives no characteristic flame? I think lead gives no distinct flame. But Pb(OH)2 is white, does not dissolve in NH3, and PbS is black, not white. So not lead.

Al3+ gives no flame, Al(OH)3 white, does not dissolve in NH3, and Al2S3? Not typical, but Al sulfide is not stable in water, may produce white precipitate? Not sure. But (NH4)2S with Al3+ may produce no precipitate because Al3+ forms complex? Actually Al2S3 hydrolyzes to Al(OH)3 and H2S, may not precipitate. So white precipitate suggests not Al.

Thus likely Mg2+ or Ca2+. Flame test no color eliminates Ca. So Mg2+.

Thus salt likely MgCl2. However MgCl2 is soluble, but we observed white precipitate with KOH (Mg(OH)2) and with (NH4)2S (MgS) white. Good.

Check if MgS is white? Yes, magnesium sulfide is white. So consistent.

Thus answer: cation Mg+2, anion Cl-.
